inline.s: Grief is the chief thing in mourning. Killing is the chief of crimes. To spread a feast in the place of weeping only fills the living; to lay out lavish cauldrons before the coffin only adds to the karma of resentment. Therefore at a funeral one must not take life.

In the sacrifices of spring and autumn, and in the offerings made to the departed on the anniversary of the death, the aim is simply to pour out the blood-sincerity of the descendants. Yet one ought only to release living creatures in order to dissolve old offenses. How can it be fitting to kill and so create fresh calamity? Therefore at a sacrifice one must not take life.

When men fall ill, they kill living creatures to sacrifice to the spirits and pray for help. They do not consider that, wishing to live themselves, they instead kill other lives to keep their own alive. If the spirits truly had numinous power, would they come and accept such offerings? Therefore in prayer and sacrifice one must not take life.

Equality is the Buddha; uprightness is the god. There is utterly no principle by which blessing descends because of a bribe. When men today make a vow and then slaughter to fulfil it, this is called an evil vow. Even if it succeeds as they wish, inauspicious recompense follows. Therefore in making vows one must not take life.

When man and wife first marry, this is the heir of ten thousand generations, the source of birth after birth, on which the ancestral temple depends. Yet today men kill and slaughter to the utmost of their will, planting a wicked cause of future vengeance; they gather the urge to kill inside the women's apartments. Therefore in marriage one must not take life.

Host and guest pledge and offer toasts, and no cry of grief is heard from the chopping block; laughter fills the hall, and no one sees the misery within the cauldrons. Plainly the ancients' meaning in the words two viands suffice for the offering is one we may take as our model. Therefore in entertaining guests one must not take life.

Heaven does not bring forth men who have no emolument. If one has a single skill or a single art, one can in every case get food and get wealth. Why take such pains to ply the knife and push the blade? Moreover, the more one kills, the poorer one becomes. Therefore in making a living one must not take life.

To cut up birds and beasts to fatten one's own body: what distinction is made between the wise and the dull? To cook blood and flesh to fill one's own belly and guts: the inversion is extreme. And besides, fat and oil are soon exhausted, while the karma of resentment still remains. Therefore in providing nourishment one must not take life.

To kill one life in order to keep one life alive is what a benevolent man will not do; and besides, death and life are fixed by fate, so it is by no means certain that the other life will be kept alive. To harm creatures while curing an illness only adds enemies of resentment after death. Therefore in using medicine one must not take life.

The sick seek ease, just as creatures hate to be killed. Men today say that the lives of creatures are hard to prolong, and that reason requires them to be cooked and carved; would they then also say that since a man is ill and disabled he may be put to death? Therefore in nursing the sick one must not take life.

When the Daoist rites of offering are finished, the ceremony turns to giving thanks and sending off the generals: for the greater ones, a sheep and a pig; for the lesser, the three victims. Would the gods and sages, for the sake of a trifling mouthful, send calamity upon those who cultivate merit and virtue? Therefore in giving thanks to the generals one must not take life.

The custom of late, on New Year's Eve, is for the greater households to kill a sheep and steam a pig, and for the lesser to use fowl, fish, and a pig's head. Do they not know that when the old year ends and spring begins, it is the very time when all the gods and the ancestral spirits come down together to look upon them? Therefore on New Year's Eve one must not take life.

At the first setting forth toward rank and fame, when the heart of benevolence is at its fullest flow, how can one bear to let living kind die young and so store up hidden pain? To waste and destroy is to injure life; to be proud and extravagant is to ruin virtue. Therefore on a glorious occasion one must not take life.

In sending a gift, the original intent is a fine courtesy; but rich and fresh fare stirs the urge to kill. For oneself, one kills for a crowd and alone bears the guilt; for the other, one gives free play to a single bout of eating and earns no merit for it. Therefore in making gifts one must not take life.

How can a farewell feast be without feeling? Plain soup has its own flavour. Why be extravagant in a moment of heaping plenty, and so gather the wailing of great flocks of creatures? Therefore at a farewell feast one must not take life.

Those who feed goldfish bring in nits and shrimp by the ten thousand; those who feed white cranes bring in tiny fish by the hundred thousand. The great, delighting ear and eye, have a karma of killing stored up in this. Therefore in amusements and hobbies one must not take life.

What has been said above speaks only of the general outline. Men should take this and extend it. Then within the square inch of the mind there will be the measure that covers all under Heaven and bears all upon Earth.

Huang Luzhi's verse says: My flesh is the flesh of living beings; in name we differ, in substance we do not. We share one and the same nature; only the bodily form is apart. Their suffering they must bear; the fat and sweet are what I require. Do not let King Yama pass the sentence; search your own heart, and see what you are.

Think: yesterday they swam, leaped, and soared; where have they gone today? Dimly one sees the flying, calling, drinking, and pecking of their living days, and already they have melted into the bowl. These words are most kindly and compassionate.

Xu Zhenjun. As a boy he loved hunting. Meeting a fawn, he killed it. Beside it was a doe, which licked it for more than an hour and could not bring it back to life; in grief it leaped and died. Zhenjun cut it open and saw that its intestines were torn inch by inch. Thereupon he threw down his bow and sighed, saying: How sad! That even among the creatures the love of nature's kind should reach this pitch! So he went away and studied the Way, aiding men and benefiting creatures, and realized the fruit of immortality.

Zhang Yizhi of the Tang had an iron cage made, and put geese and ducks inside it; in the middle he raised a charcoal fire to roast them. Around the edge he set vessels holding a broth of the five flavours. The geese and ducks ran around the fire, and when thirsty drank the broth; when the broth was gone he added fire, until the feathers fell and the flesh was cooked, and then he took them out and ate them. Afterwards he was put to death by Zhang Jianzhi.

Ren Tianyi, a merchant of the West, was greedy of profit and cruel. Every year he went to the Qingkou district of Haizhou and slaughtered and salted pigs; afterwards he would load the pigs and cross the Liuan lock at Gaoyou. One night a great wind overturned his boat; the pigs were scattered as the fishermen scrambled for them, and Ren on the bank cried out in bitterness. The great mast of the capsized boat fell across his body and crushed him into a meat pie. Now, if wealth is in one's fate, it may be got anywhere; why must one do these deeds that take life and harm life? There are very many whose retribution is like that of the merchant Ren. Men should examine themselves, and must never seek a living only to walk instead the road of death. As for robbers burning and plundering, and men drowned in the waves, these too are perhaps no more than Heaven repaying killing with killing.

Zhu Pei of the Song loved to keep pigeons, and a cat ate them. Pei caught the cat and cut off its four feet; it cried out for several days and died. Afterwards the son born to him had neither hands nor feet. Again, Zhou Ang was taking a nap by day when on a beam there was a swallow's nest, and three nestlings were chirping as they waited to be fed. Ang was angry, and fed them cocklebur; their breasts split and they died. Afterwards his three sons were all mute. Again, Zhang Lin was angered by the croaking of frogs and poured hot ashes over them; afterwards he himself died suddenly, scalded to death by hot water. Put these together and observe them: can a man bear to do cruel harm to creatures? And having done it, can he escape the retribution of guilt?

Patriarch Lü of the Tang said: If you would prolong life, hear my words; in all things be wakeful and forgive yourself. If you would prolong life, you must release living creatures — this is the true principle of the round of cause and effect. When another is to die, if you save him, then when you are to die, Heaven will save you. To prolong life and beget sons there is no other way: abstain from killing and release living creatures, and that is all.

Qi Xidu. Juechu says: Pull out one hair, and the four elements are shaken; burn one moxa cone, and the whole body suffers pain. For one body is itself the body of the body of all, and living beings are the very life of my own life. Since blood and breath are thus bound up together, how can misery and sorrow leave me untouched? Yet again men take that fat and sweet fare and give free play to their own mouth and belly. Think: yesterday they swam, leaped, and soared; where have they gone today? Dimly one sees the flying, calling, drinking, and pecking of their living days, and already they have melted into the bowl. Then though the eight dainties be spread before one, all are cries of woe and karma of resentment; though the five cauldrons stand in a row, all are wandering spirits in torment. Naturally the heart grows tender, and how could one swallow again? More than that, the arm draws back, and one cannot dip a finger in. If one is thus warned and touched at every hour, and holds it in mind in every thought, then the compassion and joy of one substance arise, and the mark of living beings no longer appears; the Able One's universal rescue embraces every body that has awareness. Juechu says: Chicken, pig, leek, and taro — meet them and eat them. This seems to make a lasting topic of talk. To bury the dead and nourish the living, one takes creatures for the offering, as if one held it for a standing ordinance. Do they not know that the weak are meat for the strong, and that even other kinds hate to be wounded and maimed? Those who have received breath and contain life, those who have awareness — are they willing to be chewed? Only because, from the first cry on the ground and the very swaddling clothes, one grows accustomed to what is rich and savoury; before the prenatal state has fallen away, the womb has already grown used to rank and rank-smelling. Fish from the pond and ducks from the garden are served daily in the household kitchen; pigs from the pen and sheep from the fold are laid before the chopsticks at every hour. Because of that perfuming habit, through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand turns, greed and gluttony grow, increasing day by day and month by month. Try for yourself: before a dish has entered your teeth, once you lift your chopsticks you feel yourself hesitate; and if you meet with a rare thing not used in daily fare, once in the mouth you are mostly doubtful and afraid. Thus the men of Wu and Yue relish frogs, while a man of Qi, seeing it, has his hair stand on end; the men of You and Yan are fond of scorpions, while a scholar of Yue, seeing it, is chilled at heart. Is this because their tastes are by nature so different? Truly it is that the burden of habit makes them unlike. If one truly considers that, sharing one nature, one cannot bear to wound that nature, and that living creatures are not meant to feed the living, then once the long-sealed knot is opened, the six senses at once become pure. The net of desire, layer upon layer — the diamond sword, without being wielded, of itself splits it; the many urges to kill — the land of long life, without being trodden, of itself is ascended. I beg you, hear these words of habit, and you will surely have an awakening. Juehui says: The maggot relishes the filth it carries — how is that different from a platter heaped before one with delicacies? Carrion thrown to an owl — what distinction from three fresh fishes set out in a row? For taste is made by karma, and so when karma is heavy the mind drowns in a craving for scabs; is flavour born of the nature? When the nature is twisted, the liking turns to chasing stench. Consider the kite and the fox eating wild carrion: one covers one's sleeve, unable to bear even to watch; flies and gnats swarming on rank meat: the eye catches it and one thinks of vomiting. How is it then that amid silken strings and pipes men race to set out a hundred thousand sea-delicacies, and in a hall of brocade and damask seek out rare mountain dainties beyond number? Fragrance and savour are like the dung-beetle rolling its ball; heavy repletion is like a hog's relish for rot. At the extreme, when the bell has sounded and the water-clock is run out, the stench of fish still clings to the teeth; and when the music ends and the wine is done, the rank foulness of the garments turns the nose. Truly consider: can the pure dharmakāya admit the tastes of the five turbid world? Creatures of blood and breath — all are impure, all are foul. Then the mind that drowns in craving will of itself be swept away day by day and dwindle day by day.

Jueyin says: When a being of feeling receives its fruit below, the principle of cause and effect is no lie; raise a sound and the echo follows it, so how could the workings of karmic condition fail? The fuel is spent and the fire passes on; the fuel at last returns to fire. The string is drawn and the arrow flies; the arrow must come from the string. For the gift proceeds from that other, and its recompense comes back; the giver should indeed forget the thought of it. Yet the root is planted by oneself, and the planter ought to have good fruit. Therefore, though the wise man may set down the white ring and the pair of treasures with no thought in his heart, before the furnace fire and the cauldron of boiling water he is often filled with dread. But there are those who give free play to their own insatiable greed and maim the ever-living creatures about them. They roast fish and broil turtles, never thinking of the cauldron of oil boiling a hundred times; they cut flesh and burn lamb, and straightway sip a slice of delicate mince. More than that, they chase the wind and race the lightning, with the strong bow and the black call; they empty the marshes and exhaust the woods and thickets, until the birds lose their mates and fly off in terror, and the beasts leave the herd and are left alone. This is to crave every living thing without exception, to have one's tongue licking the sky; such a man has already become a wolf or tiger among men. As for one who must seize whatever creature there is, whose eye has already fallen to the ground — can he escape becoming a hawk or hound among beasts? Truly consider: of the ten thousand kinds that rise and sink, not one is without feeling; all that lodge their substance between the two principles alike think of requital. I vow that from today I will forever cut off old enmities, so that there is no grudge to repay and no fruit of manifold sickness is summoned; where there is peril I will surely save, so that the cause of long life comes of itself. With one wakeful thought, one does not lose the ten years of a water-buffalo; with three lives clearly seen, how could one fall to be a wild fox for five hundred? This is the peerless good affinity, the precious raft on the road of delusion. Hear my glib tongue, and you should turn your head of yourself. Juehui says: There is coming and going, and the succession of living kinds is impermanent; there is no extinction and no birth, and the compassion of my own nature is freely at ease. Therefore, seeing them alive, one cannot bear to see them die; the benevolent and the sage alike take this as their hearts' ground. Sparing them when they are destroyed, one must surely rejoice when they are brought to completion; for all living beings equally receive one nature. Thus even tiles and pebbles are without feeling, yet the man of understanding still loses his voice when a jar is dropped; and the wriggling worm has awareness — how then could the perfected man take delight in maiming life? Moreover, from the egg to the nestling, from the nestling to the feathered bird, the toil of feeding it in the mouth — how can it be a single call or a single peck? And from nothing it transforms, and from the transformation it comes to be; the liveliness of the living impulse — how can it be a single night or a single morning? Yet men take ten years of rearing and provide only the kitchen knife of a single morning; with a hundred schemes of search and snaring they furnish only a moment of drunken repletion. Do they not consider that once broken, a life cannot be joined again? The minced body and flesh, piece by piece, is a bearing of sorrow toward its end; and once destroyed, how can it be made whole again? Limb parted and body seared, thing by thing all carry pain as they go to their end. Now, the five grains are provided for man, and even of those a single grain is hard to consume; how much more do living beings each hold their own lives — how can one wildly destroy so much as a hair's tip? Truly remember: the dead, through ten thousand kalpas, can never live again; while I who eat — in a single instant it has already turned to nothing. They are seeking life and cannot obtain it; how then could one look upon their death and be content? Forever practise compassion, and let pity endure for long. Then, without waiting for the pair of shoes to be set upon the head, one has already saved the cat; and there is no need of a single promise to open the throat before the goose and the jar are both preserved. This is the true principle; how could it be an empty saying? Let it be yet more widely proclaimed, and may all alike give rise to the thought.

Yin zei. To wound another by secret plot is yin zei, as when a hidden arrow wounds a man: nothing is harder to guard against. And the man is harmed by me, yet I bear no name for evil. Such a one is chief among the goblins and sprites. To do this to anyone else is wrong; to do it to the good and virtuous is especially wrong. For the good and virtuous are the hope of the people: if they are in a single state, that state holds them weighty; if they are in a single district, that district holds them weighty. Can such be secretly wounded?

Li Linfu of the Tang was chief minister. Insidious and unfathomable, he secretly wounded the good and the virtuous, and his evils are too many to recount. When he was about to fall, he saw a ghostly thing with saw-teeth and hook-claws, a body of hair and lightning eyes, which struck Fu with its hand. Before long Fu died, blood flowing from all seven openings. After his death the court by decree stripped him of his rank, broke open his coffin, and mutilated the corpse, and banished his sons and grandsons to Lingnan. In the early Chunxi era of the Song, at Hanzhou, a woman was struck dead by thunder; on her body were written in red: Li Linfu, as a minister, was disloyal, secretly wounding the good and virtuous; for three lives a harlot, for seven lives an ox; when the recompense is done, he shall forever fall among the water-creatures. When a petty man secretly wounds a gentleman, if he happens to succeed in his scheme he says that life and death lie in his hand. He does not know that the death of those who die by his hand is also brought about by their own resentment and hatred, and is not something he is able to accomplish. If the gentleman had no resentment or hatred, then let the petty man do what he will, in the end he cannot kill him. And the wicked man who harms others is like one who spits at the sky: the spit does not reach heaven, but falls back upon himself. The worthy cannot be destroyed; the calamity will surely destroy oneself. So it is likewise here. Yet the two words secret wounding need not always belong to those in office; all other men have them too, and among the clerks of the yamen they are most extreme. What is called drawing up a bill of particulars, buying up a false denunciation, laying an evil fire, sending an anonymous letter. Do they not know that the Way of Heaven loves to return what is given, and that before one has wounded another one has already wounded oneself? Think it over, think it over.

An means the place where men neither see nor hear; wu means to cheat. This sentence is aimed especially at those who love reputation and those who counterfeit feeling. The grace of ruler and parent is the same as that of Heaven and Earth. If one receives emolument and shirks his work, covets profit and bends to private ends, or with wicked flattery gives free play to his deceit — and this heart cannot be shown to his ruler — that is secret contempt of the ruler. If one's provision for one's parents is not sincere, and one's conduct is unworthy, or one glosses over and conceals one's disobedience — and this heart cannot be shown to one's parents — that is secret contempt of one's parents. Disloyalty and unfiliality, harming the teaching and rebelling against the Way — what can surpass these? In life one meets Heaven's calamity; in death one is tortured in the courts of darkness. There is surely no escape.

Yin Hejing of the Song, when about to attend the imperial lecture, would always bathe and sit upright, and, in his court robes, bow twice to the book he was to expound the next day. When men asked him why, he said: If one would surely move his ruler and father by what one says, how can one fail to exhaust sincerity and reverence?

Emperor Xuanzong of the Ming loved letters and composed poems, and often commanded his assembled ministers to match his rhymes. A certain academician, conceited of his high talent, whenever he finished a poem by imperial command would say: Such a fine poem — the Emperor could not write it, and how could he even appreciate it? Before long, because the characters of a poem violated the temple taboo and the words touched on mockery, he was condemned for irreverence and stripped of office.

In the Three Kingdoms period, the famous scholar of Wu, Gu Ti, whenever he received a letter from his father, would kneel to read it, answering yes to each sentence in turn. If his father was ill, he would weep over the letter, his voice choking as he spoke. Again, Fan Xuan of Jin, at the age of eight, happened to injure his finger and cried loudly. Someone said: Why such pain? Xuan wept and said: It is not for the pain. This body, skin, and hair I received from my parents, and I dare not injure it; that is why I grieve. Both men afterwards rose to eminence.

There were two brothers who took turns to support their mother, five days each. The elder was poor and the younger somewhat better off. When the elder supported their mother, gruel was scarce; two days of his turn were lacking, so he told his mother to go to the younger brother's house for the time being, and he would make up the days when his turn came. The mother went and told him the elder's intention. The younger ordered his wife to hide the rice and firmly refused her. The mother then returned in tears. Suddenly thunder and lightning broke out, and the husband and wife were both struck dead. Alas, for the disloyal and unfilial, there is open punishment and hidden execution, and ten thousand years of spitting and cursing. The misery of the retribution is like this. For ruler and parent stand first among the five relations; therefore in serving ruler and serving parent above all one must make sincerity the first task.

A teacher is one who transmits the Way, confers learning, and resolves doubt. Our parents give us our bodies; but a teacher must also complete our learning. Therefore the honor due him is the same as that due to parent and ruler. When men today engage a tutor for their sons, they mostly put on empty show: they stint their wealth and fall short in courtesy, or even use disrespectful words and behave abnormally, deliberately slighting him. Such men are truly not far from birds and beasts. As for the teacher himself, in opening the understanding of a youth his hidden merit is the greatest. How then can he receive a man's tuition and offerings and yet be self-indulgent and lax, so that the talents of others suffer from failure to be brought to completion? To write their exercises in their stead, to deceive father and elder brother, to covet wealth, to bribe their way to rank and fame — I do not know what the retribution for this will be. To be slack toward a teacher is of course wrong; but for a teacher to be held in contempt by others is also wrong.

Emperor Ming of the Han had Huan Rong as his teacher, and fulfilled sincerity and reverence toward him to the utmost. The Emperor visited the office of the Grand Master of Ceremonies and had Rong seated facing east; he set out a stool and staff for him, and gathered the hundred officials to honor and revere him.

You Zuo and Yang Shi of the Song studied together under Cheng Yi. One day they went to pay their respects; Yi happened to be sitting with his eyes closed. The two disciples stood in attendance. When Yi awoke, the snow outside the door was more than a foot deep. Not the least sign of sloth was on their faces, and their reverence grew more scrupulous. The two disciples thus transmitted the learning of the Lian and Luo masters.

Peng Ruli of the Song had Ni Tianyin as his teacher, and served him with the utmost reverence. Afterwards both Ni and his wife died, leaving no son. Peng buried them, and moreover married their daughter to the presented scholar Song Huan.

Yue Wumu of the Song had Zhou Tong as his teacher, and could draw a bow of three hundred catties. When Tong died, on the first and fifteenth of every month he would set out offerings before the grave, kneel, bow, and weep. He would take up the bow Tong had given him, shoot three arrows, and only then return.

A certain farming family had a son, and wished him taught to read, with the keenest intent. Yet they treated his teacher with incomparable rudeness and disrespect. Their fare was only vegetables, and the tuition fee was always paid in debased silver. The teacher trained the boy with all his heart for a long time; when the boy read other men's essays he understood them clearly, but when he wrote his own there was nothing to be commended in them. Strange indeed! Afterwards he still returned to farming.

A certain teacher was by nature much afraid. One of his pupils was clever and unruly; he pasted paper into a giant's head and raised it outside the wall at night. The teacher was terrified, broke open the door and fled to a friend's lodging, and was ill for three days before he could rise, and in the end dared not go back to the school. Afterwards this pupil was again outside the wall and saw a giant's head. Thinking it was the one he himself had pasted, he went up to look; then its eyes moved and its beard bristled. The pupil fell dead of fright.

The way of serving a teacher should be like a younger brother's service of an elder brother, or a son's of a father. Walk behind him; sit at his side. Meeting him on the road, stand upright and join your hands. When he speaks, listen with inclined ear and empty heart. Though there be regret or remorse, sorrow or anxiety, do not change toward him; in good fortune and bad, in calamity and blessing, be one with him. In life, keep the rites strict at every half-step; in death, mourn him in the heart for three years. If one can do this, one is near to it.

A certain Wang, in instructing young beginners, always exhausted heart and strength, and did not haggle over his fee. He often said: Heaven, Earth, ruler, parent, and teacher — these five stand side by side. Once a boy has become my pupil, his success or failure, honor or disgrace for a whole lifetime rests on me. If I do not exhaust my heart and strength and so ruin another man's son, that is the same guilt as a bungling physician's killing of a man. He also loved to tell the boys stories of filial piety and brotherly respect, saying: The learner puts the heart's ground first and letters and arts afterward; he makes firm the root first and then extends benevolence. If filial piety and brotherly respect are wanting, though a man's talent shake the world, he is not to be esteemed. In his later years he begot the Duke of Literature, Kang; men took this as the recompense of good teaching.

In recent times the way of the teacher has fallen low, and one could truly weep and heave great sighs over it. Do they not consider that to ruin another man's son will surely provoke the gods to censure? Long ago there was a scholar past sixty who said to his wife: Though I have not risen in the world, happily I have had fine teaching posts all my life, and so I have made a home and built a livelihood. By night he dreamed that his father reproved him, saying: You were a man destined for the examinations; only because you were slack in your duty at your teaching post has Wenchang struck away your roll of laurel. And you still boast? Ah! From this we see that those who ruin other men's sons stand in peril indeed.

Shi means to serve one's superior from below, as a subordinate official serves his superior, a private soldier his general, a servant or concubine the master of the house — all these are shi. Pan does not necessarily mean open rebellion; it is enough that when urgent need comes he is not one to be relied on, and in matters of gain and loss he feels no concern for you — that is already called pan.

In the Three Kingdoms period, Lu Bu served Ding Yuan, by whom he was treated with great favor. Yet for Dong Zhuo's sake he killed Yuan. Having then served Dong Zhuo and sworn to be father and son to him, he again killed Zhuo for Wang Yun's sake. Afterwards he was taken by Cao's soldiers. Cao wished to let him live; Liu Bei said: Does the Illustrious Duke not see how Lu Bu served Ding and Dong? Cao understood, and ordered him strangled.

Yang Zhong of Siming was the servant of Dai Xianke. Dai was very rich, and made Zhong steward of one of his estates, which was abundant in the profits of fish, salt, bamboo, and timber. When Dai died, his son Bojian was young and fond of the company of worthless young men; within a few years the family was ruined, and only that one estate remained. He went to live there, and Zhong made an inventory of its goods and wealth and presented it to him. Bojian was delighted, and squandered as before. Zhong wept and remonstrated, but was not heeded. One day the companions of his rounds came again, and they held a drinking party and called for the gaming board. Zhong came forward with a blade in his hand and dragged out the chief among them, and counted off his faults, saying: I have served my master for more than thirty years. The young lord is young, and you men have led him into evil. The family is already ruined; happily I have preserved this estate. Must you surely squander it too? I will cut off your head, denounce myself to the officials, and beg for death, to answer to my master beneath the earth. The man admitted his guilt and begged that from today he would not dare come again. Then Zhong sent him away with several lengths of silk. Weeping, he apologized, saying: Your old servant has alarmed and offended the young lord. I beg that from today you change what you have done before, and only let your old servant exhaust heart and strength in your service; in no more than two or three years the old estate can be restored. Otherwise your old servant must at once drown himself in the sea, for I cannot bear to see the young lord starve to death and bring shame on the household. Bojian was ashamed, and wept and followed him. In a few years he indeed wholly recovered the lands and house. Zhong afterwards enjoyed a great old age. I have heard that Shen Hengji of Wu commandery once kept a dog. Afterwards Hengji fell ill, and the dog at once stopped eating. When he died, the dog howled loudly and did not stop until the whole night was over. A year later, at the burial, the dog dashed itself to death beside the grave. How righteous was that dog! Those men who in the face of life and death change their conduct and turn their hearts are truly lower than a righteous dog.

Men without understanding should be awakened as the occasion arises: warn them by principle and right, move them by good and evil, and bring them to awakening so that they do not fall into delusion. How could one deceive them because they are easy to cheat? The Surangama Sutra says: To dazzle and delude the ignorant, to mislead living beings in doubt — after death one falls into the unintermitted hell. Alas, why should men take such pains to do this?

Liu Hefeng said: Three men were walking together when they came to a stream. The water had risen, and the boat was on the far bank. The middle one of the three was by nature simple, and the others persuaded him to strip off his clothes and swim across to fetch the boat. He came and went through the rushing water and got across; then he poled the boat back to ferry the two others over. As the two stepped into the boat, the simple one suddenly had a stomachache and wanted to relieve himself, and hurried ashore. The two at once waved their hands and said: The sun is already setting; we cannot wait for you. And so they poled away. In a moment the water ran swift and the boat swung broadside, and both were overturned and drowned. The simple one stood on the bank, untroubled as before.

Jiang Fu of the Tang, dressed in a Daoist's cap and robe, entered the capital. Since no one knew him, he lied, saying he was several hundred years old and possessed the art of long life and of passing beyond the world. He served Emperor Xuanzong, received imperial favor, and was famed for a time. Afterwards a certain imperial university student, Jing Yan, went to see him and asked: Sir, of what age are you? He said: I am a man of the Liang dynasty. Asked whether he had held office, he said: I was once military commissioner of Xiliang prefecture. Yan shouted at him: How can you lie so wildly, cheating the Son of Heaven above and deluding the world below? The Liang dynasty was south of the Yangtze; where could there have been a Xiliang prefecture? There were only the generals of the Four Pacifications, Four Pacifyings, Four Punitive Expeditions, and Four Garrisons; where could there have been a military commissioner? Fu had no answer, was deeply ashamed, and died a few days later.

Bai Cen met a strange man and obtained a highly effective prescription for a boil on the back. A certain courier officer wished to transmit his prescription and spread its relief everywhere, and offered him several tens of pieces of gold. Cen gave him a false prescription, which did not cure the illness. Afterwards Cen was eaten by a tiger, and left the true prescription on the road; the officer passed by and got it.

A certain diviner Zhang was skilled in astrology, but for the most part gauged men's intentions and cast his reckonings mostly not by the rules. Sometimes he took secret commissions from people and turned his readings upside down, ruining men's great affairs. Afterwards he bit through his own tongue and died.

Wei Zheng happened to buy fish. The seller moved the balance and secretly gave Zheng extra. When the fish-seller had gone, the master of the shop said: Sir, you bought only five catties, and I have secretly doubled it. I beg you to give me wine. Zheng was greatly shocked, pursued the fish-seller and paid him the value, then drank the shopkeeper's wine and said: What you wanted was only wine — why cheat a poor man? Alas! If men today had Wei Zheng's heart, how could there be any deceiving of the ignorant?

Fellow students are friends whose affection is that of brothers. Moreover, friendship holds one place among the human relations; how can one wildly heap slander on a friend, and store a bellyful of spears and halberds?

The Buddha said: In their dealings with friends, men owe one another five things. First, if either does an evil deed, each should dissuade the other. Second, if either meets with trouble or illness, each should look after him and nurse him. Third, if either has words of family confidence, he must not speak them to outsiders. Fourth, each should respect and praise the other, never breaking off their comings and goings, and must not keep grudges. Fifth, if one is poor and the other rich, one should support and relieve the other, and they must not slander one another.

Someone asked: After one has taken a friend, one learns that he is not good. To break with him wounds the affection; not to break with him is to harbor resentment while yet being his friend. Master Zhu said: That is not harboring resentment. To have resentment in the heart while outwardly associating with him — that is harboring resentment. If a friend is not good, affection and right of themselves require that one draw away; only draw away gradually. If there is no great cause, why must one cut him off sharply? And one should accumulate sincerity to move him to awakening. This is what is meant by saying that toward kin one does not lose the way of kin, and toward old friends one does not lose the way of old friends.

Wang Shouren, Master Yangming of the Ming, said: In friendship, humility and deference are the chief thing. When friends meet, one must empty the heart and bend the will, treating the other with affection, respect, and forbearance. On the whole, there should be little admonition and fault-finding, and much of the sincere wish to move and encourage. Wen Jiexiao said: In friendship one takes only the other's strengths and does not reckon his shortcomings. Meeting a blunt, unbending man, endure his harsh temper; meeting a brilliant, unrestrained man, endure his reckless temper; meeting a plain, generous man, endure his sluggish temper; meeting a frivolous, clever man, endure his flighty temper. Not only does one gain beyond measure; this is also the way to keep a friendship whole.

Zhang Qianzai of the Song, styled Yi'e, was a friend of Wenshan. When Wenshan was in honor, he repeatedly summoned him, but Qianzai would not come out. When Wenshan was defeated and returned to Jizhou, Qianzai slipped out to see him and said: If the Prime Minister goes to Yan, Qianzai goes too. He went and lodged close by the prison, and for three years his provision was never lacking. On the day Wenshan was executed, Qianzai secretly hid his head in a coffer. Having learned that his wife, Lady Ouyang, was among the captives, he burned the corpse, gathered the bones, and placed them in a bag, and with the coffer went south, delivering them to the family for burial. The day before, Wenshan's son dreamed that his father said: I have returned with Yifu. Soon afterward he indeed arrived. Later men called this the friendship of life and death: Qianzai the one osprey. Truly so. Shen Zhonghua said: To betray a dead friend does greater harm to right than to betray a living one. Let those who make friends today ask themselves whether they can keep an unchanging heart through life and death.

Guo Zhi of the Song first won fame for his rhapsodies. His fellow student Li Mian, envying him, slandered him, and because of this Guo Zhi repeatedly failed in the examinations. Afterwards Zhi was graduated first and twice presided over the examinations, while Mian was still being chosen on the strength of the classics. On the day the decree came down, Mian, ashamed and repentant, went home. Zhi heard of it and hurried to call him back, and Mian in the end took his degree. From this one may see that slander does no harm to the other man; it only brings meanness upon oneself.

To speak without any ground is xu, emptiness; to lay on another a stain he does not have is wu, false accusation; to deceive men by a cunning scheme is zha, fraud; to counterfeit feeling and cheat the world is wei, falsity. Divided, they are four words; joined, they are simply insincerity. Sincerity is the Way of Heaven; to think of sincerity is the Way of man. Now to cast aside sincerity and be empty, false-accusing, fraudulent, and false — is that not to rebel against the Way of Heaven and lose the Way of man? The heart is greatly toiled, and the affairs greatly endangered; this is the first of all the world's marks of scant blessing. If such a man does not enter the three evil paths, where else shall he go? Sun Tingquan of Yidu in the Qing was plain and sincere, without ornament, and so the Shizu Emperor used to call him Honest Sun. Whenever there was a vacancy in a ministry, he would always say: We had better use Honest Sun. Three times he said Honest Sun, and Sun was made a grand secretary. When did honesty ever mislead a man?

Xue Fu made a specialty of fabricating false plaints, able to dress up the unreasonable as reasonable, and by this he grew rich. Afterwards he held a rite of offering to atone for his guilt. The Daoist priest bowed, then rose and said: The Most High has written at the foot of your memorial: The household is given to the fire office; the man is given to the water office. In the end his house was burned to ashes in a fire, and Fu fell into the water and died.

Xue Wenjie of Min in the Five Dynasties had a grudge against Wu Ying. One day the ruler of Min, Lin, had a shaman look for ghosts in the palace. Jie first said to Ying: The ruler suspects you of holding too much power. You may plead illness. If an envoy comes to ask after you, answer that you have a headache; I can speak for you. Ying agreed. Jie instructed the shaman to say that Ying was about to rebel, and that the Most High had nailed his brain with a copper nail. The ruler sent an envoy to verify it, and Ying indeed answered that he had a headache. So he was killed. Ying had been falsely accused, and the people ground their teeth. It happened that Lin sent out troops against Wu, and the soldiers would not advance; they wanted Xue Wenjie handed over before they would march. Lin had no choice but to send him in chains to the army, where he was cut to pieces on the spot.

Zhao Tingchen of the Song made a false agreement with the cave tribesmen that they should submit to the court; he made them drunk and killed them, then proclaimed that they had rebelled, and seized the merit for himself. Zhao was thus conspicuously promoted. Afterwards he dreamed that the man he had killed said: I have come to repay your fraud. A son was then born to him, who in youth passed the examinations, and by his mad and rebellious lawbreaking brought his father to ruin: Tingchen and his wife were sentenced to banishment beyond the mountains, and were killed by the cave tribesmen.

Ding Wei of the Song never spoke a true word to anyone. He once said: If a man's heart is honest, he can accomplish nothing, and will only suffer others' contempt. Wei set his heart in this way, and so it was fitting that none could fathom him; yet the world all marked him out as one of the Five Ghosts. Was it that his false heart did not reach far enough?

Those of the same surname are called clan; those of other surnames are called kin. Though near and far, close and distant, are not equal, in truth they are all persons bound up with my own body. One should treat them with affection, loyalty, and sincerity, sharing their troubles, relieving their want, hiding one another's family shame, and together fending off insults from without. How then can one contend with them, each against the other, reckoning every hair's difference, with resentment and jealousy, overthrowing and snatching, spying and denouncing? He who breaks off a branch wounds the heart of the tree; he who cuts the root severs its vein. Be warned.

Yan Pingzhong of the Spring and Autumn period drove a shabby carriage and a lean horse. Huanzi thought he was concealing the ruler's gift. Yanzi said: Since I came to honor, there is no one in my father's clan who does not ride in a carriage; no one in my mother's clan who lacks food and clothing; no one in my wife's clan who suffers cold or hunger. Of the scholars of Qi, more than three hundred wait for me to light their fires. Is this concealing the ruler's gift, or making it known? He put his father's clan first, his mother's clan next, then his wife's clan, and only last those more distantly related. This is what is meant by extending to those one does not love the love one bears to those one does. Yanzi may be called good at bringing his kindred into harmony. If men had such a heart, could the vice of denouncing one another exist? I therefore set this down as a rule for those who denounce others; and the evil retribution of denunciation need not be recounted in further cases.

The firmness and resolution that Confucius approved is governed by principle; the rigidity and strength that the Most High warns against is stirred by temper. Physicians call the numbness of palsy by the name not-benevolent, because the sufferer has no sense of pain or itch. The man who loves to be hard and give rein to his temper, in his treatment of men and things, has no sense of pain or itch; he is nothing but an urge to kill. What the vulgar call an iron-hard heart, that is what he is. How can he be benevolent? Yet there is none so rigid and strong who is not in the end broken. If a man has swallowed a few great losses and gradually softens into gentleness, that is the greatest good fortune of the rigid and strong. I look for it daily.

Bao Zheng of the Song was academician of the Dragon Diagram Pavilion, and was given the posthumous name Xiaosu. Inwardly firm and unbending, when his subordinates made reports he often rebuked them to their faces; yet whenever what they said hit the principle, he never failed to correct himself with good cheer. Therefore all men submitted to him. To be firm and yet near to principle, and to be able to decide matters when they come — this is the courage of the benevolent.

Zhang Ruqing of the Song was a judicial commissioner. Whenever he tried a prisoner, whether the crime were grave or light, he applied every punishment in turn, and called it playing a full set. Those who underwent his interrogation said that Yama had called them to account. Afterwards, when his term was full and he was returning home, his boat lay at Gaoyou; by night he dreamed of several hundred men with broken heads and snapped legs, surrounding him and demanding his life. When he reached home, he saw fierce ghosts in broad daylight, and died with blood flowing from all seven openings. That the violent do not die a natural death need hardly be said; but how long must one wait to be freed from the retribution of the three paths after death? Extending the thought from this case, all who are hard in a way that comes near to cruelty, or strong in a way that sinks into thievery, may also take warning.

In whatever a man does, if he employs others he is wise; if he employs only himself he is foolish. To rely on oneself is already wrong; how much more to be fierce and violent. The Buddha said that the fierce and violent are like a wicked horse — meaning that they are hard to tame. When a man is fierce and violent, obstinate in everything, thinking himself right, unwilling to yield to others, then what good friend or wise teacher will come near him? What good words, what true principle, will anyone tell him? Of the sources that produce evil and invite blame, none is greater than this.

Wang Anshi of the Song was envious and jealous, masking evil with pretended goodness, banding with his own party to attack those of different views, and using stubborn argument to becloud the truth. He placed himself on a level with Gao, Kui, Ji, and Qi. His administration ruined men of talent; his learning ruined men's hearts. In his Three Classics and his Explanation of Characters he slandered and maligned the sages and shattered the great Way, and not in one matter only. The Spring and Autumn Annals rectifies names and ranks and fixes praise and blame, so that rebellious ministers and villainous sons are afraid; Anshi made scholars give up the Spring and Autumn. The Records of the Historian and the History of the Han set out success and failure, safety and danger, survival and ruin, order and chaos, and are the mirror of the ages; Anshi made scholars give up reading the Histories. Yang Xiong did not die when Wang Mang usurped the throne, but wrote his Drama on Qin and Praise of the New; yet Anshi said that this accorded with Confucius's nothing that may not be done. Feng Dao served four dynasties and eight rulers; yet Anshi said he was good at avoiding trouble and preserving himself. He had the ministers and high officials all take his words as their model, so that there was no spirit of integrity or loyalty. At first he was on good terms with all the worthies; because they disagreed over the new laws he drove them all out. His son Pang even said: Hang the heads of Han Qi and Fu Bi in the marketplace, and the new laws will be carried out. The rest may be known from this. Afterwards, because those who attacked him grew many, he became only more arrogant, fierce, and reckless, saying that the changes of Heaven were not to be feared, that men's words were not to be heeded, and that the laws of the ancestors were not to be kept. His guilt was heavy and his evil full. One son, Pang, fell ill with a boil on the back and died young; his grief was more than he could bear, and he repeatedly pleaded illness and asked to leave. Shenzong in the end grew weary of him, and he was dismissed from office. Above he lost his ruler's favor; below he grieved that his heir was cut off; in between he was hated by men. The worthies he had driven out came one after another into power and wholly abolished his laws. He died of shame and fear.

The gentleman makes abundant the trunk of benevolence and right, and makes firm the dike of propriety and righteousness. Then he can weigh with fairness what is to be loved and hated, and settle aright what is true and false. For true and false, in one man, decide that man's worth; in one district, decide that district's weal or harm; in the empire, decide the empire's safety or peril. How can one fail to be careful, and by rashness settle what is not right, calling right wrong and wrong right?

Yin Shilu of the Song, in his own conduct and in teaching others, called right right and wrong wrong, concealing and avoiding nothing, never stopping for convenience and never following for convenience, intent only on exhausting the principle to the end. At the point of death he sent a handwritten farewell to Duke Fan Wenzheng. Wenzheng hurried to him; the Duke had already bathed, put on cap and sash, and sat upright and passed away. Wenzheng wept bitterly. The Duke opened his eyes again and said: I have already taken leave of you; why have you come again? Life and death are the constant principle; why does Xifan not understand? Having spoken, he bowed again and passed away. Lord Yin was a student of his time. Had he not exhausted the most subtle and refined, then at the threshold of life and death there would have been many things rising up to disturb him. In entering the Way, knowing and doing are used together, and knowing is the chief. This is what is meant.

Cai Jing of the Song was chief minister. He enrolled the chief ministers and executives of the Yuanyou and the end of the Yuanfu eras, Sima Guang and others, the attendant ministers Su Shi and others, the civil ministers Cheng Yi and others, and the military ministers Wang Xianke and others, one hundred and twenty men, as a wicked faction, and asked the Emperor to write it out and have it carved on stone at the Duanli Gate and in every prefecture and county. The people were all indignant. Before long the stele was shattered by a thunderbolt, and Jing was banished for an offense and died in exile.

Xiang means that to which one ought to turn: the so-called good men and good deeds. Bei means that which one ought to turn away from: the so-called wicked men and wicked deeds. To turn to the wicked and turn away from the right is called perversity. A single moment's fault ruins a whole lifetime. How can one fail to be careful?

Tang Shenxi of the Tang was chief minister under Wenzong. Because Zheng Zhu wielded arbitrary power, he wished to remove him, and having as his friend Wang Fan, who was the magistrate of the metropolitan district, he secretly had him watch for Zheng Zhu's unlawful acts. Fan, because Zheng Zhu was in favor, meant to inform on him. Zheng Zhu was afraid, and in turn falsely accused Shenxi of treasonous designs; Shenxi was banished to be adjutant of Kaizhou and in the end died nursing his indignation. Afterwards Lady Song dreamed that Shenxi led her outside the city to a pit. In the pit were several condemned prisoners. He drew one of them forward and showed him to her, saying: This is Wang Fan. I have already petitioned the Most High about him. Then, in wrath, he shouted aloud, and she started awake, and silently took note of it. Before long Li Xun and Zheng Zhu plotted to put the eunuchs to death, and memorialized that they should go to the Jinwu guard to view the sweet dew; they sent Fan and others with troops to kill them. Fan's thighs trembled and he dared not advance, and the affair ended in failure; he was cut in two at the waist in the marketplace. Several who were executed with him were all buried in the same pit outside the city.

Liu Zhongsu, whose name was Zhi, of the Song once argued against the ten harms of the labor-service commutation. Wang Anshi reproached him for turning and turning away perversely, and sent the case down to the Directorate of Agriculture, with an edict ordering him to explain himself. The Duke said: That to which I turn is loyalty and uprightness; that from which I turn away is wicked flattery. That to which I turn is right; that from which I turn away is profit. That to which I turn is my ruler and father; that from which I turn away is powerful villainy. That I should be condemned for this I had already reckoned in myself. Yet the commutation of labor service will in the end harm the empire; I beg Your Majesty not to forget my words. All men clicked their tongues for the Duke, and the Duke alone paid no heed. Afterwards he became chief minister. Master Lu said: To turn to what one ought to turn to — the turning is not for private ends; to turn away from what one ought to turn away from — the turning away is also for the public good. He had never reckoned on fortune or calamity; yet fortune and calamity followed from it. This too is a warning to those who will not be Lord Liu but are content to be Wang Fan.

When a candle meets the night, it accomplishes the work of breaking the darkness; when a boat gets water, it accomplishes the work of carrying things. In general, when the water arrives the channel is formed, and the merit will show of itself; there is no need to go and seize it. If one has a mind to seize it, then all the generals who let their troops plunder and kill, the officials who wildly add to taxes and corvée, and the judicial officers who put many men into crime, may all act as they please without the least scruple. But all such men exchange the fat and blood of the common people for one man's merit and fame. The merit is got, to be sure, and it is no more than promotion; but calamity comes too, and not only the loss of life. A man, though exceedingly foolish, would never go so far as this. Do we not see the ancients? Cao Bin of the Song, coming down to Jiangnan, put not one man to death. Ji An of the Han, with a false imperial order, opened the granaries and kept several tens of thousands alive. Yu Dingguo of the Han, as chief justice, so ordered matters that the people of themselves felt no wrong had been done them. In their own day, were these men not the foremost of ministers?

In the time of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang, expenditures grew daily more extravagant, and he did not wish to draw on the treasuries of the left and right. Wang Hong, a vice minister of revenue, understood the imperial mind, and so squeezed the common people, sending in each year a hundred million in extra coin and silk beyond the assessment, which was stored in the inner treasury for the Emperor's use. The Emperor thought him able to enrich the nation, and promoted him to be investigating commissioner of the capital region; soon after he was promoted further to vice minister of revenue and prefect of the metropolitan prefecture. Yet within and without there was lamentation and resentment. Before long he was brought down by the affair of his younger brother Han, and was given death.

Wang Shao of the Song proposed opening the Xihe region, and many were killed. He accumulated merit until he became privy councillor. He had also deliberately killed the old and young of surrendered Qiang tribesmen, taking their heads so that his relatives and friends might steal the merit and receive titles. In his later years he repented, and asked the elder masters about cause and effect. All of them said that killing by the king's law is like a boat crushing snails and mussels as it goes: it is done without intent. Only Diao Jingchun said: I fear only that you cannot get the better of your own heart. If you can get the better of it, you will not need to ask. Shao was all the more afraid. Afterwards a boil broke out on his back, and he called out for the countless men with cut-off heads and severed legs who were demanding his life; his chest burst and he died. His eldest son vomited blood and died; his youngest son was beheaded for an offense, and his house was extinguished.

Zhang Wu and others, commoners of Zhenyang county, stole an ox. A neighbor, Hu Da, and others arrested them. Zhang Wu was beaten to death by Da. The remaining thieves instead reported to the county that they had been robbed. The magistrate Wu Miao, wishing to claim the credit, impeached Da and eleven others for robbery and murder; under cruel torture they falsely confessed. Among them two men, Zhu Kui and Zhang Yun, died of illness. When the case had been reported to the prefecture, it was sent down to the judicial commissioner. At that time Zhang Wengui was judicial commissioner of Yingzhou. He observed that the prisoners' words and looks gave grounds to doubt the truth of it, and on a single interrogation he got the facts. He also seized the gang of ox-thieves as witnesses. When the case was complete, Hu Da, for killing a thief in pursuit, was sentenced to beating on the back; the rest to beating on the buttocks; and Kui and Yun were innocent. Wu Miao's scheme came to nothing, and he vomited blood and died. Afterwards Wengui suddenly fell gravely ill and came to a government office where the presiding officer asked him about Wu Miao's case. He answered with the facts. The presiding officer said: I already know this matter in full detail; it is only necessary that you come and complete the testimony, for the value lies in examining the truth. Far off he saw Wu Miao, in cangue and chains and bowed to the ground, with Kui and Yun standing beside him. A clerk brought out a document and showed Wengui the foot of the page, where there were three characters: add one twelve-year cycle. He woke, and at once recovered. In later years, at seventy-eight, he again dreamed that a spirit said: I formerly added twelve years to your span, and you have now also mitigated one man's capital crime to strangling; another half cycle shall be added. In the end he died at eighty-three.

Chan means to flatter and fawn; xi means to abet and assist. When the ruler's mind is not yet settled, it may still be turned back. Only when men come fawning on him does it grow firm and immovable. This is not only the minister toward his ruler; it is likewise when a subordinate official caters to his superior, a gentleman to the government office, a clerk to his own magistrate, a servant or concubine to the head of the household. All who hold a higher place should in every matter follow principle, and must be careful not to be greedy for their own private advantage, so that others find a crack to slip in by. And those below: how can they seek rank and fame by unreasonable means, or covet unrighteous wealth, knowing only to fawn and egg on, servile of face and kneeling on bended knee, so that they merely lose their own hearts and knit up endless karma of resentment?

In the Xuande era of the Ming, the eunuch Wang Sanbao was sent down to the Western Seas and other foreign lands to seek rare treasures. In the Tianshun era someone memorialized that he be sent again, and the court ordered the Ministry of War to examine the earlier records. Xiang Zhong was then at the Ministry of War, and ordered a clerk to examine them. Liu Daxia, a director, went first to the storeroom and hid them; the clerk found nothing, and the proposal was dropped. Xiang reproved the clerk, saying: The documents are in the storeroom; how can they be lost? Lord Liu smiled slightly and said: When the voyages were made before, they cost several hundred thousand in coin and grain, and the soldiers and people who died were beyond counting. Even if treasures were got, they did the nation no good. This is a corrupt practice, and it is what a great minister ought to remonstrate against with all his strength. If the old records still existed, they ought to be destroyed to uproot the matter. Why still ask whether they exist or not? Lord Xiang apologized, saying: My shallow understanding did not reach so far. Words such as yours move Heaven by their hidden merit; this seat ought to belong to you. And so it turned out.

Emperor Taizong of the Tang once pointed to a tree and said: This tree is very fine. Yuwen Shiji chimed in and praised it without ceasing. The Emperor said with a stern face: Wei Zheng urged me to keep flatterers at a distance. I did not know who the flatterers were; now I know that it is you. Shiji knocked his head on the ground and in shame begged pardon.

Guo Chongtao of the Later Tang, wishing to please the mind of the Zhuangzong Emperor, urged the establishing of Empress Liu. His intent was to ingratiate himself. Afterwards the one who slandered Chongtao to death was none other than Empress Liu. To abet the ruler's wish and urge the establishing of an empress, meaning thereby to secure himself, and instead to bring down so cruel a calamity — what good did the flattery do?

For the kindness of a single meal the ancients were sure to repay. Even when repayment was beyond their power, the heart was sure to engrave it and be moved. They held it in mind and kept it before them, and could not let it slip. The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: To receive kindness and feel no gratitude is worse than a beast. How true a saying! Yet kindness has its greater kinds: first Heaven and Earth, second father and mother, third ruler, fourth teacher. There are men who muddle through a whole life without repaying these four kindnesses, and yet are smugly pleased with small private favors and petty benefits. This is again to cast away the root and chase the branch, and such a one is no repayer of kindness.

Shi Wuwei of the Tang was a friend of Zhang Congzhen. Wuwei's family was poor, and Congzhen would every week give him clothing and food, and supplied him with capital to trade, and in a few years he grew rich. Then Congzhen's house was burned and his whole estate was emptied. He went to Wuwei, and Wuwei in the end betrayed their former friendship. Congzhen could only sigh and sob toward Heaven. Suddenly black clouds rose up and thunder struck Wuwei, who was changed into an ox, and on its belly was written in red: The ungrateful Shi Wuwei. In ten days he died. The saying goes: Even beasts know to repay kindness — the horse drags the rein, the dog spreads the grass, the snake brings the pearl, the sparrow carries the ring in its beak. Creatures are still like this; how can a man betray virtue? And is he not afraid of being changed into an ox?

Zhang Bi of the Song was tranquil and unassuming and fond of learning, and was skilled in the Book of Changes. He rescued Li Daliang from a difficulty. When Daliang rose to honor, he met Bi on the road, held him and wept, and offered him all the wealth of his household; Bi refused and would not accept. Daliang said to the Emperor: That I have come to serve Your Majesty was the work of Bi. I beg to give him all my rank and title. The Emperor promoted Bi to be a director, and then commander of Daizhou. Bi did not take the kindness to himself, and Liang was sure to repay the kindness; both were right.

For the enmity of ruler or father, for hatred among flesh and blood, the gentleman has his own way of repaying resentment with uprightness. As for private enmities and small grudges, they may be dismissed by principle and forgiven by feeling; they should simply melt like ice. If one broods on them without cease, then resentment will repay resentment, and when will it ever end?

Li Deyu of the Tang, as chief minister, made many enemies. Afterwards he was banished to Zhuyai, and saw on a temple wall more than ten gourds hanging. He asked the monk, who said they were men's bone-ashes: when the Grand Commandant was in power, he banished and drove out his colleagues in his grudges, and they died here; the old monk pitied them and burned their bones, waiting for their sons and grandsons to come and claim them. Deyu, hearing this, was startled and turned to flee, and died of a heart attack.

Jin Cheng of the Ming was a secretary in the Ministry of Justice. Before he had risen, he had once been put to shame by Ma Zhang. Afterwards Zhang committed a crime and was sent in custody to the capital. Catching sight of Cheng, at every step he made nine stumbles. Cheng greeted him with a smile and saved him from his guilt. When Zhang came to pay his respects, Cheng received him with the rites of ordinary times. Zhang was moved to tears, and gave his daughter in marriage to Cheng's son.

Yu Tieqiao once said: When men press me with power and circumstance, I bear with them by the measure of my own forbearance; thus one sweeps away layer upon layer of cloud and puts out a spark of fire. So the gentleman does not remember old wrongs.

inline.s: 47. He treats with contempt the people of Heaven, and throws the government of the nation into disorder.
48. He rewards what is unrighteous, and punishes the innocent.
49. He kills men to seize their wealth, and overthrows men to seize their place.
50. He puts to death those who surrender and slaughters those who submit; he degrades the upright and pushes aside the worthy.
51. He oppresses the orphan and presses hard upon the widow.
52. He casts aside the law and takes bribes.
53. He calls the straight crooked, and the crooked straight.
54. He makes light offenses into heavy ones.
55. He adds anger to one who is being put to death.
56. He knows his faults and does not reform; he knows what is good and does not do it.
57. He lays his own guilt on others, and blocks up the arts and methods of others.
58. He rails at and slanders the sages and worthies.
59. He encroaches upon and bullies the virtuous.

60. He shoots the flying and hunts down the running; he breaks open the burrows of hibernating creatures and startles those at roost; he fills up their holes and overturns their nests; he injures the unborn and breaks the eggs.
61. He wishes others to fail, and destroys the success of others.
62. He endangers others to secure himself, and diminishes others to benefit himself.
63. He exchanges the bad for the good, and sets aside the public for the private.
64. He exposes men's ugliness, and denounces men's private secrets.
65. He wastes away men's goods and wealth.
66. He separates men's flesh and blood, encroaches on what men love, and aids men in wrongdoing.
67. He gives free play to his will and puts on a show of power; he humiliates others to win the victory.
68. He ruins men's crops, and breaks up men's marriages.
69. If he is rich, he is proud; if he escapes, he is shameless.
70. He claims the kindness for himself and shifts the blame to others; he shifts disaster onto others and sells evil to them.
71. He buys empty praise, and stores up a treacherous heart.
72. He thwarts what others are good at, and shields his own shortcomings.
73. He uses his power to coerce and threaten, and gives free rein to violence, killing and wounding.
74. He cuts and tailors without cause, and cooks and kills against propriety.
